title: Values With an Even Digit Count
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers. Return how many of them are written with an even number of digits in base 10.

Count by position: if the same value appears twice and qualifies, it counts twice.

examples.why: 42 has 2 digits and 1000 has 4. 7 and 305 have an odd count.
10 and 99 have 2 digits, 100000 has 6, and the second 10 counts again.

gen: (r, big) => [Array.from({ length: big ? 500 : r.int(1, 8) }, () => r.int(1, 10 ** r.int(1, 5)))]
hints: How do you count the digits of a number without turning it into a string?
Divide by 10 until the number reaches 0 and count the steps. Then check the count with % 2.

explain.intuition:
The digit count of x is how many times you can divide it by 10 (rounding down) before it becomes 0. Strings give the same answer with String(x).length, which is the quick way in an interview unless you are asked to avoid it.

Because values are at most 100 000, you could also just compare against ranges: 10–99, 1000–9999 and exactly 100000 are the even-length ones.
steps: For each value x, count its digits by repeatedly dividing by 10.
If the count is even, add one to the answer.
pitfalls: Using x / 10 in JavaScript without Math.floor. The loop then runs until floating point underflows.
Counting distinct qualifying values instead of every position.

solutions.title: String length
solutions.idea: Turn each number into a string and check the parity of its length.

solutions.title: Count digits by dividing
solutions.idea: Strip digits with integer division by 10 and count how many steps it takes.

followups: Values can be up to 10¹⁸. Which approach still works in JavaScript, and why?
Count the digits in O(1) with a logarithm. Where can floating point rounding bite?
